topicDisplay: An Introduction to Philosophy of Religion
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Arguments for the existence of God
The problem of evil and suffering

questions.q: The cosmological argument for the existence of God is also known as the:
questions.explain: The cosmological argument claims the universe must have a first cause, which believers identify as God.

questions.q: Which thinker is linked with the design argument and its analogy of finding a watch?
questions.explain: William Paley argued that just as a watch implies a watchmaker, the order in nature implies a designer (God).

questions.q: The design (teleological) argument concludes that order and purpose in the universe point to:
options: An eternal universe with no beginning
questions.explain: The design argument reasons from apparent order and purpose in nature to the existence of an intelligent designer, God.

questions.q: A person who believes that God does not exist is best described as a(n):
questions.explain: An atheist is someone who does not believe in the existence of God or gods.

questions.q: An agnostic is someone who:
options: Believes it is not possible to know whether God exists
Is certain that God does not exist
questions.explain: An agnostic holds that the existence of God can neither be proven nor disproven, so it cannot be known for certain.

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the cosmological argument?
options: Everything that exists has a cause, so the universe must have a first cause
The beauty of nature shows it was designed
Belief in God brings people comfort
Moral rules must come from a lawgiver
questions.explain: The cosmological argument reasons that since everything has a cause, there must be an uncaused first cause, God.

questions.q: A student looks at how precisely an ecosystem is balanced and argues this could not have happened by chance. Which argument is she using?
questions.explain: Arguing from order and apparent purpose in nature to a designer is an example of the design (teleological) argument.

questions.q: Evil and suffering caused by human actions, such as murder and theft, is called:
questions.explain: Moral evil is suffering brought about by the deliberate choices and actions of human beings.

questions.q: Suffering caused by nature, such as earthquakes and floods, is called:
questions.explain: Natural evil is suffering that results from the natural world rather than from human choices.

questions.q: The problem of evil is often expressed as a difficulty in holding together three beliefs: that God is all-powerful, all-loving, and that:
questions.explain: The 'inconsistent triad' questions how an all-powerful, all-loving God can coexist with the reality of evil and suffering.

questions.q: The term 'omnibenevolent' means that God is:
questions.explain: Omnibenevolent describes God as being wholly and perfectly loving.

questions.q: The term 'omnipotent' means that God is:
questions.explain: Omnipotent means all-powerful, that God can do anything that is logically possible.

questions.q: The free will defence responds to the problem of evil by arguing that:
options: God gave humans free will, and evil is a result of people choosing wrongly
God is not powerful enough to stop evil
Suffering is always a punishment from God
questions.explain: The free will defence says God allows moral evil because genuine freedom to choose good requires the possibility of choosing evil.

questions.q: A powerful storm destroys homes and crops, causing great suffering. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Suffering caused by natural forces rather than human choice is classed as natural evil.

questions.q: When a friend is seriously ill, a Christian says the experience may help to strengthen their faith. Which response to suffering is this?
options: Seeing suffering as a test that can build faith
Claiming that God does not exist
Arguing that evil is an illusion
Denying that the friend is really suffering
questions.explain: Many Christians believe suffering can be a test or opportunity to grow in faith and trust in God.

questions.q: A miracle is usually defined as an event that:
options: Breaks the laws of nature and is believed to be caused by God
Can be fully explained by science
Is a normal part of everyday life
questions.explain: A miracle is commonly understood as an event that appears to break natural laws and is attributed to the action of God.

questions.q: Which philosopher argued against belief in miracles, claiming they are the least likely explanation of an event?
questions.explain: David Hume argued that it is always more probable that a report of a miracle is mistaken than that a law of nature has been broken.

questions.q: The sense of awe and wonder felt in the presence of a holy or divine reality is described as the:
questions.explain: The numinous refers to the feeling of awe, wonder and mystery experienced in the presence of the divine.

questions.q: A conversion experience is best described as one in which a person:
options: Changes their beliefs and commits, or recommits, to a faith
Sees a natural law being broken
questions.explain: A conversion experience is a religious experience that leads a person to change and commit to a faith or renew their commitment.

questions.q: A person suddenly changes their whole outlook and dedicates their life to God after a dramatic religious event. This is best classed as a:
questions.explain: A dramatic experience that leads someone to change their life and commit to God is a conversion experience.
